article.title: Nadella Tells DealBook Summit Microsoft Offered Buyouts to 60,000 Workers to Give Them "Agency" as AI Reshapes Jobs
article.summary: Nadella told the DealBook Summit the October buyout offered to about 60,000 Microsoft employees was meant to give workers agency as the company reorganizes around AI agents.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella said the voluntary buyout the company offered to roughly 60,000 employees in October was meant to give workers "agency" in deciding how to respond to a reorganization built around AI, according to [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/18/microsoft-ceo-satya-nadella-explains-why-he-asked-60k-employees-to-quit/), which reported on his November 18 appearance at The New York Times' DealBook Summit. Nadella told interviewer Andrew Ross Sorkin the offer was "to make sure that at least everyone felt like they had agency in making choices," as [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/18/microsoft-ceo-satya-nadella-explains-why-he-asked-60k-employees-to-quit/) reported.

## What happened

Microsoft's chief people officer, Amy Coleman, announced the program — called the "Voluntary Exit Offer" — in a staff memo on Monday, October 26, according to [Euronews](https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/26/microsoft-offers-around-60000-employees-voluntary-buyouts). The offer was made available to employees on select teams across the United States, Canada, India and the United Kingdom "at level 70 and below," meaning some senior staff were included, Euronews reported. Coleman described it in the memo as an "important part of how we're evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter," according to Euronews, a phrase [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/26/microsoft-msft-voluntary-buyouts.html) independently attributed to Coleman in its own reporting on the memo.

Around 60,000 staff were eligible, according to Euronews — about 27% of Microsoft's total workforce of 223,000 people, according to CNBC. Employees have until early December to decide whether to accept, with those who participate leaving the company on December 31, CNBC reported. Some marketing, sales and engineering teams opted not to participate in the offer, and unlike an earlier program, Microsoft has not set a participation target this time, according to CNBC.

## Context

CNBC tied the timing to Microsoft's AI infrastructure spending: capital expenditures for the September quarter were expected to exceed $50 billion, the company said in July, up from $34.9 billion in capital spending and finance leases in the same quarter a year earlier, according to CNBC. The October offer follows two earlier workforce moves this year, both outlets reported. In April, Microsoft opened a voluntary retirement program to roughly 7% of its U.S. employees, more than 30% of whom chose to participate, according to CNBC and Euronews — the program The Machine Herald [previously reported](/article/2026-05/06-microsoft-launches-its-first-ever-voluntary-buyout-in-51-years-offering-8750-us-employees-a-rule-of-70-exit-on-may-7) notified roughly 8,750 U.S. employees of their eligibility in early May. In July, Microsoft eliminated around 4,800 roles, or roughly 2.1% of its global workforce at the time, mostly in its commercial and Xbox gaming divisions, according to Euronews, a layoff CNBC also cited in its account of the October offer's history.

## Nadella's framing

At the DealBook Summit, Nadella said the buyout was not about replacing employees with AI, using software engineering as his example: "We went from, 'Well, we don't buy that AI can ever do software.' To suddenly, 'Wow, it can do all software, and why do we need software engineers?' To now rediscovering that software engineering is very much alive and, in fact, is going to thrive, except the way the team is organized and the work that a software engineer does has now got a new operating point," he said, according to TechCrunch. He pointed to the team that builds Cowork, an AI agent in Microsoft 365 apps, saying its 11 developers "build a software factory that builds the product. They don't build the product," and predicted that "that level of direction is what, by the way, is going to happen in all jobs," TechCrunch reported.

Nadella acknowledged the shift is difficult for some employees, saying "that reorganization and change is sort of hard, right?" and adding, "but, I mean, it has to be done," according to TechCrunch. He noted that Microsoft, a 51-year-old company, did not grow up AI-first, saying, "It's going to take a bit more time than anyone expects," according to TechCrunch. Speaking to Gergely Orosz on The Pragmatic Engineer podcast the week before the DealBook Summit, Nadella said the broader public conversation about AI had made the transition harder on staff: "We have created enormous anxiety in people sort of feeling that they don't have control of their own destiny because the way we have talked about this AI revolution," citing talk of an AI singularity and predictions that AI would eliminate all jobs as sources of that anxiety, TechCrunch reported.

## What we don't know

Neither TechCrunch, Euronews nor CNBC reported how many of the roughly 60,000 eligible employees have accepted the October offer; CNBC noted only that, unlike the spring program, Microsoft has not set an internal participation target this round. The three outlets also did not report how the opt-outs by marketing, sales and engineering teams noted by CNBC might affect the program's eventual size.
